correctness.rationale: Define weighted medians as observed values, with strict uniqueness on both sides of each initial center. Positive affine order equivariance proves the medians along the candidate trajectories. Their derivatives exactly match every agent equation, and full initial data are recovered. Prior global Lipschitz guarantees uniqueness; the exact proof covers every finite \(m,n\), positive normalized shared row weights and real initial opinions. The nearest-observed-neighbor \(K_{2,2}\) tie boundary is verified algebraically. The standalone exact-rational checker passes 1,289 admissible finite cases and four boundary rational times; it is corroboration only.

claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: The source vector field is exactly the studied one and its global well-posedness is prior art. The new asserted implication is stronger on a restricted family: all initial vectors with two unique group medians have an explicit limit and \(e^{-t}\)/\(e^{-2t}\) trajectories, with a nonunique-median boundary instance. A general convergence theorem alone does not calculate these quantities; different discrete-time models do not imply this continuous-time law.

originality.rationale: The v1 initiating paper introduces this ODE and proves well-posedness, stable equilibria, and convergence; its v3 revises and expands qualitative claims. Both were inspected for the initial-data-to-limit map and partwise median invariance. Earlier asynchronous and synchronous discrete-time median models have different update laws. Exact statements and implications, not merely keyword nonmatches, were compared. Searches found no preempting two-median finite-time formula; unindexed equivalence remains a risk.

value.rationale: A natural two-community structure supports a conserved pairwise order-statistic sum and gives a complete consensus-selection map, which qualitative global convergence does not determine. Exact \(e^{-t}\) internal and \(e^{-2t}\) intergroup transients identify different mixing timescales; robustness to nonmedian outliers and independence from group size make the invariant socially and mathematically interpretable. A four-agent tie example isolates the assumption controlling the phase transition to possible dissensus.
